To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial distribution of sediment composition (i.e. mineralogy) in modern estuarines is primarily controlled by the character of the bedrock and sediment transport in the source area and the critical grain size threshold of the mineral in question.
the distribution of detritus in estuarine sandstone is primarily controlled by the size of the grains, and the hydrodynamics in the estuarine system.

(i) detrital mineralogy in estuarine sandstone reservoirs is primarily controlled by the character of source rocks; (ii) mineralogy patterns can be used to predict reservoir quality and porosity; and (iii) mineralogy patterns in estuarine sands are primarily controlled by hydrodynamics and grain size.

the spatial distribution of primary detrital mineralogy in modern estuarines, with a view to better predicting sandstone reservoir quality in ancient estuarine sandstone reservoirs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial distribution of mineralogy and reservoir quality in ancient estuarine sandstone is predictable from modern analogues.

we have shown how the distribution of primary detrital minerals in estuarine sands can be explained by hydrodynamic and sediment transport mechanisms and the mineralogical character of the source area.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the composition of sandstone reservoirs is predictable as a result of the spatial distribution of primary detrital mineralogy.

, by understanding the spatial distribution of minerals, we can improve our ability to predict reservoir quality in sandstones, which will lead to more accurate estimates of hydrocarbon resources and more cost-effective exploration.
